references.text: This text in Exodus is the original source of the formulation in Numbers 14:18. Here the Lord reveals himself to Moses and proclaims his character as slow to anger, abounding in love, forgiving sin and rebellion, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation.

In the second commandment, the principle is mentioned that God visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation, but shows love to those who love him and keep his commands.

Moses repeats the commandments and again mentions that the Lord visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation, but shows love to a thousand generations of those who love him.
The psalmist describes the Lord with similar words: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness.
The Lord is described as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love, reflecting the description in Numbers 14:18.
The psalm praises the Lord as gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and great in loving-kindness.
Joel calls the people to turn back to the Lord, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in love.
Jonah uses the same formulation about God's character when explaining why he fled: he knew that God is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in love.
Nahum describes the Lord as slow to anger but great in power, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished.
Nehemiah quotes the same confession: God is a God of forgiveness, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in love.
Jeremiah confirms that God shows love to thousands, but repays the iniquity of the fathers on their children after them.
Paul writes about God's riches of kindness, forbearance, and patience, which are meant to lead to repentance, reflecting God's slowness to anger in Numbers 14:18.
Paul discusses God's patience toward vessels of wrath, showing how God is slow to anger even toward those who deserve judgment.
Peter explains that the Lord is slow to anger and does not want anyone to perish, but that all should come to repentance.
